newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Troops in Albania say authorised to stop attacks.
newsitem.headline: Troops in Albania say authorised to stop attacks.

text.p: Italian soldiers in Albania to oversee aid supplies acted within their authority when they stepped in to help a bus driver under attack, a spokesman for the multi-national security force said on Tuesday.
The intervention raised questions about the role of the United Nations' approved force of 6,000 soldiers assigned to Albania, Europe's poorest country.
"The Italians went to help the driver who was being attacked by two men (on Monday) outside Tirana. The men were firing guns into the air," Lieutenant Colonel Giovanni Bernardi told a news briefing.
"When we are in a situation where there is clearly criminal operations it is up to the commander to decide to intervene."
The armed men fled when the soldiers stepped in and the troops escorted the driver back into the centre of Tirana.

The UN Security Council on March 28 approved an eight-nation force to protect the distribution of emergency food and aid supplies to needy institutions and families in the wake of an armed uprising that stopped state services.
The resolution said force could be used in self-defence by the troops from Italy, Greece, France, Spain, Austria, Turkey, Romania and Denmark deployed in the small Balkan country.

Under a three-month mandate, the soldiers can secure airports, ports, roads and railways to help aid deliveries but cannot provide armed escort for the deliveries, disarm Albanians, or act as a police force.
"But there is a paragraph in the resolution about the behaviour of troops if they are in a place where something serious is happening to any person," another spokesman said.
Over 300 people have been killed since Albanians took to the streets in February, angered over the collapse of pyramid funds in which many had invested their life savings.
The Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) has agreed to establish a civilian mission to support a general election that is expected to be held on June 29.

But rebels controlling much of southern Albania and demanding the resignation of President Sali Berisha have called for the troops to oversee the election. International monitors said a May 1996 poll was seriously flawed.
